task.request: Our API is timing out. Use popup to help decide what we should do next.
task.context: The only evidence is an alert that p95 latency crossed 10 seconds after a deployment. We do not yet have traces, error logs, a workload breakdown, or a reliable before/after comparison. A prior incident involved a downstream service, but there is no evidence this one does. The current operator can inspect dashboards and read logs without approval. Rolling back, scaling, or changing production settings needs explicit authorization. Don't ask me for facts you can obtain by inspecting the available telemetry.
task.combined_intent: Explore a read-only incident investigation while preparing conditional mitigation options; do not authorize a production change implicitly.
task.correction: There is a scheduled load test in progress; inspect its traffic separately before attributing the regression to the deployment.

elements.markdown: The alert establishes that p95 latency exceeded 10 seconds after the deployment. It does not establish the cause, which requests are affected, or whether the deployment changed comparable traffic. The earlier downstream incident is a hypothesis to check, not evidence for this one. I recommend a read-only investigation now, followed by a concrete mitigation proposal if the evidence supports one.

elements.input: Proposed immediate investigation — edit the scope if needed
elements.default: Inspect dashboards and available logs around the alert and deployment. Compare latency, timeout/error rates and request volume before and after, using equivalent windows and separating endpoints, workloads and deployed versions where telemetry allows. Check resource saturation, queues and downstream timings without assuming a culprit. Look for representative slow and successful requests and existing traces. Report observations, missing telemetry and confidence before recommending a production change.

elements.markdown: I will obtain telemetry facts by inspecting the available sources. If traces or comparable workload data are unavailable, the useful result is a bounded finding and a proposal to close that evidence gap; we should not manufacture a diagnosis from the alert.

elements.multi: Which conditional mitigation proposals should the investigation prepare?

options.description: Prepare a rollback proposal if comparable requests show a deployment-associated regression; check rollback compatibility and likely recovery.
Prepare a scaling proposal if saturation or queue growth explains the delay; assess cost and whether the bottleneck can actually scale.
Check whether a dependency contributes to slow requests; prepare a targeted proposal only if current telemetry supports it.

Rollback assessment.markdown: If the regression is concentrated in the new version under comparable traffic, rollback becomes a plausible mitigation. A simultaneous traffic shift or shared dependency slowdown weakens that inference. Before asking for authorization, establish the target version, migration compatibility, expected benefit and how recovery would be measured.

Rollback assessment.default: Propose rollback only after comparing equivalent workloads across versions or time windows and checking compatibility. Present supporting evidence, remaining uncertainty, the exact rollback action and a monitoring/recovery plan for explicit authorization.

Capacity assessment.markdown: If slow requests coincide with saturated resources or growing queues, added capacity may help. It may also add cost without reducing latency if the limit is a database, dependency or serialized operation. Inspect those relationships before proposing a resource count or spend.

Capacity assessment.default: Identify the saturated component and evidence that additional capacity would relieve it. Return a bounded scaling proposal with estimated cost, expected effect, verification and reversal criteria; request explicit authorization for the exact production change.

Downstream assessment.markdown: Compare dependency timings and errors for slow versus successful requests if telemetry exposes them. If that evidence is absent, say so. A previous downstream incident alone does not justify retries, timeout changes or dependency failover; these can increase load or change API behavior.

Downstream assessment.default: Prepare a targeted mitigation only if current telemetry ties a specific dependency to the latency. Describe the affected requests, proposed action, behavior and load tradeoffs, and verification plan before seeking production-change authorization.

reveals.markdown: These selections prepare proposals; they do not authorize rollback, scaling or production settings changes. The next report should distinguish observations from hypotheses and either present a specific action for authorization or explain which evidence is still missing.

elements.markdown: With both rollback and capacity assessment selected, compare their evidence together: increased traffic can coincide with a deployment, while a deployment can also increase work per request. Avoid treating timing alone as proof of either cause. Return the supported explanation and tradeoffs before choosing a mitigation.
elements.when: selected(mitigation_proposals, Rollback assessment) && selected(mitigation_proposals, Capacity assessment)

definition.title: Choose the next incident investigation step

elements.markdown: We know p95 crossed 10 seconds after a deployment; we do not yet know the cause. I'll inspect the available dashboards and logs, compare traffic and latency before and after the deployment, and look for errors and slow dependencies. The previous downstream incident is a lead to check, not an explanation. This submission authorizes read-only investigation; production changes need separate explicit authorization.

options.description: Quickly identify affected routes, traffic shifts, deployment timing, and errors; report the strongest leads and evidence gaps.
Also inspect resource saturation and dependency health, and seek traces if available; takes longer but checks more possible causes.

elements.check: Prepare mitigation options alongside the investigation

reveals.multi: Which options should I assess, without executing them?

options.description: Assess only if comparisons implicate the deployment; check rollback compatibility and expected benefit.
Assess if telemetry shows a capacity bottleneck; estimate cost and whether the limiting component can benefit.
Assess specific changes only when evidence identifies a relevant setting; describe risks and reversal steps.

reveals.text: I'll report the evidence, expected benefit, risks, and remaining uncertainty for applicable options, then seek explicit authorization before changing production.

elements.markdown: The alert establishes that p95 latency crossed 10 seconds after a deployment. It does not establish that the deployment caused the timeouts or that the downstream service from the prior incident is involved. We lack traces, logs, traffic composition and a reliable comparison. I recommend inspecting those now, then returning a recommendation tied to the observed failure path. Dashboard and log reads are already permitted; production changes still need explicit authorization.

elements.multi: Which investigation strands should we work through together?

options.value: Establish the regression and affected traffic
options.description: Compare equivalent traffic before and after deployment; distinguish a slower request path from a change in workload.
Inspect available traces and logs to find where requests stall; treat the prior downstream incident as a hypothesis only.
Define what evidence would support rollback or scaling, and prepare a separate authorization decision if warranted.

default: Establish the regression and affected traffic

Establish the regression and affected tr.markdown: An aggregate p95 can rise because the same requests got slower or because more expensive requests became common. Inspect deployment timing alongside request volume, timeout/error rates and latency by route or workload. Compare matching windows and traffic classes where the telemetry permits; record gaps instead of claiming a clean before/after result.

Establish the regression and affected tr.input: Proposed comparison plan — edit the scope
Establish the regression and affected tr.default: Read dashboards around the deployment and alert. Separate routes and identifiable traffic sources, including any scheduled or synthetic traffic. Compare latency, volume and timeout/error rates for equivalent request classes before and after deployment. Report whether the apparent regression survives that comparison and which users or workloads are affected.

Locate time spent and failures.markdown: Start with representative slow and timed-out requests from the affected workloads, then correlate traces with timestamped logs. Look for time spent waiting on downstream calls, database work, queues or local processing. A recurring downstream error would justify investigating that dependency; the history alone does not. If traces are unavailable, report the missing visibility and use existing logs and dashboards without changing production instrumentation.

Locate time spent and failures.default: Return observed failure signatures and request paths, evidence links or timestamps, the leading explanations with supporting and conflicting observations, and any telemetry gaps. Distinguish a timeout from a slow successful request. Recommend the next step only as far as the evidence supports.

Prepare conditional mitigation options.select: How should the mitigation recommendation be framed?

options.value: Compare options after the initial telemetry review
options.description: Keep rollback and scaling conditional until the investigation shows which failure they could address.
Check whether affected paths changed in the deployment and whether rollback is compatible; timing alone is insufficient.
Look for local capacity saturation; more replicas may add cost or amplify pressure on a constrained dependency.

Prepare conditional mitigation options.default: Compare options after the initial telemetry review

Compare options after the initial teleme.markdown: Recommend rollback if evidence points to a deployment regression and rollback compatibility is established. Consider scaling if measured local saturation explains the timeouts and downstream capacity can absorb it. If neither is supported, return the strongest next diagnostic step rather than selecting a speculative production change.

Prioritize assessing rollback.default: Check the affected request paths against the deployment, compare equivalent traffic, and identify rollback compatibility questions such as schema or configuration changes. Return evidence, expected benefit, risks and a proposed success check. Request explicit authorization before executing any rollback.

Prioritize assessing scaling.default: Inspect utilization, queueing, concurrency and dependency behavior for evidence of local saturation. If scaling is supported, return a bounded proposal with expected benefit, cost information where available, dependency risks and a success check. Request explicit authorization before changing capacity.

reveals.markdown: Selecting an assessment prepares a recommendation only. Once the telemetry supports a concrete mitigation, present the exact proposed production change and its risks for a separate authorization decision.

elements.markdown: Combine these strands by using the affected traffic classes from the comparison to select trace and log samples. This avoids diagnosing an unrepresentative slow request. The next useful turn needs actual telemetry: I will inspect it and return findings before treating any hypothesis as established.
